before: The event's physical cost comes in only under Landauer's principle, as a named premise: Rolf Landauer, a physicist at IBM, argued in 1961 that a computer has to give off heat whenever it throws information away, and I take that as an assumption with his name on it.

reason: Separate physical heat from instruction accounting.

before: 2. **Establishing is not free.** If the step that turns uncertified into certified has to pay, every run from uncertified to certified has paid. Proved, for any system that follows that rule. The rule isn't arbitrary: on a machine with finite memory, a certificate that can never be revoked can only be switched on by a step that merges two states, and merging is what Landauer's principle charges for whenever the machine could be in either state. Proved in [PermanentCertification.v](coq/kernel/nfi/PermanentCertification.v), with Landauer's principle as the named premise. The heat comes from that uncertainty: a machine already known to be in one state loses nothing, and [PermanentCertificationEntropy.v](coq/kernel/nfi/PermanentCertificationEntropy.v) proves both sides. A finite machine with eight states meets both premises, and both are theorems about it ([FiniteCertMachine.v](coq/kernel/nfi/FiniteCertMachine.v)).
after: 2. **The price has stated premises.** If a step that turns uncertified into certified has to pay, every run from uncertified to certified has paid. On a finite machine with a permanent reading, an instruction that raises it merges some whole states; the newly entering state need not be one of that colliding pair. Charging every merging instruction at least one mark therefore yields the toll ([PermanentCertification.v](coq/kernel/nfi/PermanentCertification.v)). This is an abstract pricing premise. A physical heat bound additionally depends on the prepared inputs and thermodynamic conditions: a known deterministic start loses no logical entropy, whereas an equal mixture of a colliding pair loses one bit ([PermanentCertificationEntropy.v](coq/kernel/nfi/PermanentCertificationEntropy.v)). The eight-state example meets the finite-state and abstract pricing conditions ([FiniteCertMachine.v](coq/kernel/nfi/FiniteCertMachine.v)); that does not measure a device's heat.
reason: Align headline with the corrected theorem and distinguish physical from mathematical examples.
